record.paper_title: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems
record.original_question: Can one devise a genuinely practical method for performing QCD path integrals with complex actions at realistic computational cost, thereby solving the sign problem rather than merely circumventing it in limited regimes? This asks both for a method that remains reliable when the action is highly oscillatory and for a criterion of success based on feasible computational scaling rather than formal correctness alone.

evidence.quote: As there is no generic method for the integral, probably there is no numerical integration method that works efficiently with arbitrary integrands.
In this sense, it is reasonable to define the problems as ‘to perform the path integral for the theory with complex action by using realistic computational cost’.
Solving the sign problem means reducing the computational cost for the path integral as much as possible by inventing more efficient numerical techniques.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a lattice gauge theory whose partition function is given by a high-dimensional path integral

  Z = ∫ D[U] e^{-S[U]},

where U denotes the gauge link variables on a finite four-dimensional lattice and S[U] is the (Euclidean) lattice QCD action including a chemical-potential term that makes S[U] complex. Because e^{-S[U]} is not a positive real weight, standard Monte Carlo importance sampling cannot be applied; this is known as the sign problem.

Devise a numerical algorithm with the following properties:

1. It computes expectation values ⟨O⟩ = Z^{-1} ∫ D[U] O[U] e^{-S[U]} for physically relevant observables O in lattice QCD at nonzero baryon chemical potential.
2. It remains reliable when the integrand is highly oscillatory (i.e., when |Z|/∫ D[U] |e^{-S[U]}| is exponentially small in the spacetime volume).
3. Its computational cost scales at most polynomially in the lattice four-volume V and in the inverse statistical error 1/ε, for arbitrary values of the chemical potential within the physically interesting regime.

Either exhibit such an algorithm together with a proof (or convincing demonstration) of polynomial scaling, or prove that no such algorithm exists under stated complexity-theoretic assumptions.
artifact.status_search_result: The sign problem in finite-density lattice QCD remains an open problem. Numerous approaches (complex Langevin, Lefschetz thimbles, tensor networks, density-of-states, machine-learning contour deformations, etc.) have made progress in restricted regimes, but as of recent reviews no general method with provably feasible computational scaling for full QCD at realistic chemical potentials has been established. The problem is widely considered NP-hard in general (Troyer–Wiese 2005), suggesting no universal polynomial-cost solution is expected.

status_evidence.title: Computational Complexity and Fundamental Limitations to Fermionic Quantum Monte Carlo Simulations
status_evidence.snippet: Troyer and Wiese show that the sign problem is NP-hard, implying that a generic polynomial-time solution is unlikely.
status_evidence.claim: A fully general efficient solution to the sign problem is believed not to exist.

status_evidence.title: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems
status_evidence.snippet: Review classifies existing methods (complex Langevin, Lefschetz thimbles, etc.) as circumventions effective only in limited regimes, and frames the practical solution as still open.
status_evidence.claim: No method currently solves the sign problem at realistic computational cost across the full physical regime.
